newsitem.title: USA: AMR, pilots to go before special board.
newsitem.headline: AMR, pilots to go before special board.

text.p: Pilots at American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, go before a special board on Thursday, opening five days of closed-door testimony in the board's effort to craft a new labor agreement both sides can accept.
American will make its case on Friday. The procedure will be repeated next Monday and Tuesday. Rebuttal is set for Wednesday.
Under the law President Clinton invoked on February 15 to stop a pilot strike less than 30 minutes after it began, the board must come up with its contract suggestions in 30 days.
American and the Allied Pilots Association (APA) have 30 more days to accept or reject the board's recommendations.
A strike is precluded during the 60 days, but if the two sides do not accept the proposals made by the three-member Presidential Emergency Board, the union is free to strike again.

Board chairman Robert Harris said he did not plan any press briefings as the board weighed the proposals made by the union and company. He said the board's comments on resolving the dispute would be issued by the White House.

Other board members, in addition to Harris, who is a former chairman of the National Mediation Board, are Helen Witt, another former board chairman, and Anthony Sinicropi, a former head of the American Arbitration Association.

The week before the strike, the two sides held five days of non-stop talks, and the pilots decided to strike after failure to resolve the size of a pay increase and whether APA pilots would fly the new commuter jets that American intends to buy.

The APA wants its pilots, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, to fly them, but American has said that to be competitive with the regional services of other airlines, it needed the commuters to be flown by pilots from another union who are paid about half that of APA pilots.
But the ATA says it fears American would gradually shift the small jets to longer routes, jeoparizing its members' jobs.
